components.text: The four measure different outcomes in different units and are not ranked. Each identifies the jump at 50, 55 or 60 under the old rules¹

footnote: All four are peer-reviewed journal versions, figures checked against the papers
notes: China's existing studies all identify the jump at the old thresholds of 50, 55 and 60. None of them measures the new policy. The four cards use different units, so I do not rank them. The first stage: Lei, Tan and Zhao, China Economic Quarterly 2010, use urban-registered people in the 2005 one-percent population sample. At 60, men's retirement rate jumps 7 to 11 points, at 50 women's jumps 8 to 13 points, and at 55 only 2 to 3 points. The jumps are modest, which says reaching the age is not the same as retiring, and that a fuzzy discontinuity design is the right frame. Care: Feng and Zhang, Feminist Economics 2018, use CHARLS and find that retiring raises the probability of caring for grandchildren by 29 points for women and 21 for men. Health: Che and Li, China Economic Review 2018, use CHNS and find white-collar retirees' chance of reporting fair or poor health falls 34 points. Spending: Li, Shi and Wu, AER Papers and Proceedings 2015, use the Urban Household Survey and find retirement cuts non-durable spending by 20 percent. Causal studies of labor supply itself are the rarer kind. Most look at health, spending and care.
